name: System Design Interviews
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: A repeatable approach to system design interviews: estimates, caching, replication, queues, CAP, a URL shortener and a feed.

lesson.intro: System design rounds show up for new-grad roles and some internships, and the skills behind them matter whenever a feature meets real traffic. This lesson gives you a step-by-step approach, the estimates and building blocks interviewers expect, and two worked designs.
objectives: Run a system design interview from requirements to trade-offs
Estimate requests per second, storage and server counts with powers of ten
Apply load balancing, caching, CDNs, replication, sharding and queues, and name their costs
Explain CAP in plain terms and choose consistency or availability per feature
Design a URL shortener and a news feed end to end

sections.title: A repeatable approach for the interview
sections.key: Drive the interview through a fixed sequence: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, then trade-offs, thinking out loud the whole way.
sections.body:
"Design a URL shortener." You have 45 minutes and a blank whiteboard. Candidates who struggle rarely lack knowledge: they start drawing databases, design for a problem nobody asked about, and run out of time. A fixed sequence fixes that, and interviewers score whether you drive.

[[visual]]

**Ask before you draw.** **Functional** requirements say what it does: create a short link, redirect. **Non-functional** ones say how well: users, latency ("redirects under 50 ms at the 99th percentile"), availability, consistency, peak load. Agree on scope and write the list down. If you realize later that you never asked about scale, pause, ask and adjust.

State trade-offs as you make them: "I'll return 302 so we can count clicks, at the cost of more traffic." There is rarely one right design, only designs whose costs you understand.

visual.title: A 45-minute budget
rows: functional list, non-functional numbers, what is out of scope
requests per second (average and peak), read to write ratio, storage per year
3 to 5 endpoints with inputs and outputs
tables or documents, keys, which store fits the access pattern
boxes and arrows, one request traced end to end
the 2 or 3 hardest components in detail
bottlenecks, single points of failure, what to monitor, the next 10x
visual.caption: In a 60-minute round, give the extra time to deep dives.

sections.tip: When you are stuck, go back to the requirements. "Which of these is hardest at our scale?" usually tells you where to deep dive.
sections.pitfall: Opening with technology ("we'll use Kafka and Cassandra") before you know the requirements. Interviewers read it as pattern matching rather than design.

check.question: The interviewer says 'Design Instagram.' What should you do first?
choices: Draw the database schema for photos and users
Ask clarifying questions about features and scale, and agree on scope
Decide between SQL and NoSQL
Estimate how many servers will be needed
check.explanation: 'Instagram' could mean feeds, stories, messaging, search and more. Clarifying features and scale first keeps you from designing the wrong system, and the estimates and storage choices depend on the answers.

sections.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
sections.key: Estimate with powers of ten (a day is about 10^5 seconds), size the system for peak traffic, and finish by saying what the numbers mean for the design.
sections.body:
1,000 requests per second fits on a couple of servers; 1,000,000 needs caching, sharding and a different conversation. You need the right power of ten, fast, with assumptions written down.

[[visual]]

The method: users times actions gives events per day; divide by 10^5 for per second; multiply by size for storage. Servers needed = peak load / one server's capacity, plus headroom. Then say what it implies:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Numbers to know
rows: 86,400, call it **10^5**: 1 million a day is about 10 per second, 1 billion about 10,000
often 2 to 5 times the average: size for the peak
a year is about 365 days; 5 years about 1,800
memory 100 ns, SSD read 100 µs, data center round trip 0.5 ms, across a continent or ocean 50 to 150 ms
visual.caption: Memory is about a thousand times faster than SSD, which is why caches matter; count cross-region calls one by one.

visual.title: A photo app: 20M daily users, 0.5 uploads and 30 feed views each, 1 MB photos

steps.label: Storage
steps.work:
10M × 1 MB = 10 TB a day
~3.6 PB a year before replicas

visual.result: Read-heavy: a cache and a CDN carry most reads, and petabytes of photos go to object storage (S3) with only metadata in the database

sections.tip: Round aggressively and keep units on every number. "10M × 1 MB = 10 TB" is easy to check; a bare 10000000000000 is not.
sections.pitfall: Spending ten minutes on exact arithmetic. Interviewers want the order of magnitude and what it means for the design, not the third significant digit.

check.question: A service receives 500 million requests per day. Using 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds, about how many requests per second is that on average?
choices: About 50
About 500
About 5,000
About 50,000
check.explanation: 500,000,000 / 100,000 = 5,000. Dividing by 10^5 is the shortcut: drop five zeros.

sections.title: Load balancers and stateless services
sections.key: Run identical stateless app servers behind a health-checking load balancer, with sessions in Redis or signed tokens and files in object storage, so any server can serve any request.
sections.body:
After a launch, traffic triples and the one server's CPU sits at 100%. A bigger machine (**vertical scaling**) has a ceiling and is still a single point of failure. Several copies behind a **load balancer** (**horizontal scaling**) is how large systems work:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Horizontal scaling needs **stateless** app servers: nothing about a user lives in one server's memory or disk. Then adding capacity means starting servers, and losing one loses nothing.

[[visual 3]]

visual.caption: Sessions and cache in Redis, data in PostgreSQL, uploaded files in S3.

rows: round robin takes turns; **least connections** picks the server with fewest requests in flight, better when some requests are slow; hashing on IP or user id pins a client
probe each server, stop sending traffic to one that fails, add it back when it recovers
L4 routes by IP and port without reading the request; L7 understands HTTP, so it can send `/api` and `/images` to different pools and terminate TLS
the balancer runs as a pair or as a managed cloud service

items.title: Shared state
points: Sessions in Redis or a signed token
Files in object storage
Servers are interchangeable

items.title: Sticky sessions
points: The balancer pins each user to one server
Load becomes uneven and deploys awkward
When that server dies, its users lose their sessions

sections.tip: Whenever you add a box, say how it fails: "If app2 dies, health checks remove it within ten seconds and the other two absorb its traffic."
sections.pitfall: Keeping sessions or uploaded files on an app server, then adding a load balancer. Users get logged out at random, and files exist on only one machine.

check.question: Why should app servers behind a load balancer be stateless?
choices: Because load balancers cannot forward cookies to servers
Because stateless servers use much less CPU
So the database can be skipped for most reads
So any server can handle any request, and servers can be added or lost without losing user data
check.explanation: Statelessness is what makes servers interchangeable: shared state lives in Redis, the database or object storage, so scaling out and surviving failures are both easy. Load balancers forward cookies just fine.

sections.title: Caching and CDNs
sections.key: Cache-aside reads the cache first and fills it on a miss; a write updates the database, then deletes the key. TTLs bound staleness, and CDNs serve static files near users.
sections.body:
A product page runs six queries, takes 120 ms, is viewed 50,000 times an hour and changes twice a day. A **cache** (in memory, in Redis or Memcached) lets repeated reads skip the slow path:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

The hard part is **invalidation**, keeping stale data from living forever:

[[visual 2]]

A **CDN** is a cache with servers in hundreds of cities: static files come from an edge near the user (150 ms becomes about 10 ms). Content-hashed names (`app.3f9a1c.js`) cached for a year make updates instant; HTML and API responses get short TTLs or none.

visual.title: Cache patterns
rows: check the cache; on a miss, read the database, store the result with a TTL, return it
update the database, then **delete** the key. Deleting is safer than setting the new value: two concurrent writers could leave the older value cached
write to the cache and the database together, so the cache stays warm
write to the cache now, flush to the database later: fast, but can lose data

visual.title: Keeping it fresh
rows: bounds staleness: with 5 minutes, data is at most about 5 minutes old even if a delete is missed
refreshes data that must be current
`product:42:v7`: a new version simply uses a new key
a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once: let one request rebuild while others wait or get the stale copy, and jitter TTLs

sections.code:
CACHE_TTL = 300  # at most ~5 minutes stale

def get_product(pid):
    key = f"product:{pid}"
    cached = redis.get(key)
    if cached is not None:   # hit
        return json.loads(cached)
    product = db.fetch_product(pid)  # miss
    redis.set(key, json.dumps(product),
              ex=CACHE_TTL)
    return product

def update_product(pid, fields):
    db.update_product(pid, fields)  # 1. DB
    redis.delete(f"product:{pid}")  # 2. key
sections.tip: Say what staleness each piece of data can tolerate: "a product description can be five minutes old; a bank balance cannot."
sections.pitfall: Adding a cache with no TTL and no invalidation plan. Sooner or later a user sees data that is days old and nobody can explain why.

check.question: In cache-aside, what should happen when a product is updated?
choices: Update only the cache; the database catches up on the next read
Leave the cache alone and let the TTL fix it eventually
Update the database, then delete the product's cache key
Flush the entire cache so nothing stale remains
check.explanation: The database is the source of truth, so write it first, then delete the key so the next read loads fresh data. Updating only the cache risks losing the write, waiting for the TTL serves stale data, and flushing everything causes a stampede.

sections.title: Databases at scale: replication, sharding and CAP
sections.key: Replicas add read capacity and failover but lag behind the leader; shard on a key that matches the main query; during a partition, choose consistency or availability per feature.
sections.body:
The database usually buckles first, because app servers are easy to multiply and data is not.

[[visual]]

**Sharding** (horizontal partitioning) splits the rows across databases when one machine cannot store the data or absorb the writes. Pick a **shard key** that matches the main access pattern: shard chat messages by a hash of `conversation_id` and loading a conversation hits one shard.

[[visual 2]]

Cross-shard joins and transactions get hard and resharding is painful, so shard only when the numbers demand it.

**CAP** in plain terms: when a network partition splits your nodes, each side either refuses requests it cannot confirm are current (**consistency**) or keeps answering with possibly stale data (**availability**). Without a partition, the everyday trade-off is latency versus consistency.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Replication terms
rows: accepts every write and streams changes to the others
applies the leader's changes and serves reads: add followers for a read-heavy app
followers apply changes asynchronously, milliseconds to seconds behind, so a fresh edit can seem to vanish
send a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write
promoting a follower when the leader dies

items.title: Hash-based shard key
points: hash(key) mod N, or consistent hashing
Spreads data and load evenly
Range queries must ask every shard

items.title: Range-based shard key
points: user names A to F on shard 1
Keeps ranges together
**Hot spots** when activity clusters: shard by date and today's writes all land on one shard

visual.title: Pick per feature
rows: Selling the last seat on a flight
availability, with **eventual consistency**: replicas converge after the partition heals

sections.tip: Name the consistency each feature needs: "Payments need strong consistency; the follower count can be a few seconds stale." That shows more understanding than reciting CAP.
sections.pitfall: Sharding by a key that does not match the queries, such as message timestamp when you always load by conversation. Every read fans out to every shard, and today's shard takes all the writes.

activity.title: Why resharding hurts
activity.prompt: Think of each bucket as a database shard and each key as a user id. Insert eight or so keys and note which bucket each lands in. Then resize and watch how many keys move to a different bucket. With plain hash mod N, changing N moves most keys, which is why resharding is painful and why consistent hashing exists.

check.question: A user edits their bio, refreshes, and sees the old bio for a few seconds. Reads go to asynchronous followers. What is happening?
choices: The CDN is caching the database
Replication lag: the follower has not yet applied the write
The leader silently rejected the write
Sharding stored the bio on two different shards
check.explanation: The write reached the leader, but the follower serving the read has not caught up yet. Routing a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write (read-your-writes) hides this.

sections.title: Queues, async workers and rate limiting
sections.key: Put slow work on a queue for idempotent background workers, and protect services with rate limits such as a token bucket, which allows bursts up to its size.
sections.body:
Transcoding an uploaded video takes four minutes. Waiting would time out the request, and a thousand uploads would drown the servers. Do slow work **asynchronously** through a **message queue** (Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, or a log such as Kafka):

[[visual]]

You get fast responses, a buffer for spikes, workers that scale on their own and retries after crashes. Typical uses: emails, media processing, reports, webhooks.

[[visual 2]]

**Rate limiting** caps requests per client to stop overload and abuse. The **token bucket** holds up to N tokens, refilled steadily; each request spends one, and an empty bucket returns `429 Too Many Requests`:

[[visual 3]]

A **fixed window** (100 per minute, reset on the minute) is simpler but lets a client send 100 at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00; **sliding windows** smooth that. With many app servers, keep counters in a shared store such as Redis.

messages.label: already processed? skip
messages.detail: else transcode, mark ready in the DB

visual.title: What you must handle
rows: **At-least-once delivery**: a crash before the ack means redelivery
make consumers **idempotent**: check whether video 981 is done, or rely on a unique constraint
**Poison messages** that always crash a worker
after a few failures, move them to a **dead-letter queue** for a human
**Ordering**: many queues do not guarantee it
say how you keep it if it matters (Kafka keeps order within a partition)

visual.title: Token bucket: capacity 10, refills 1 per second
visual.result: Bursts up to 10, but the long-run rate never exceeds 1 request per second

sections.tip: Whenever a request does slow work the user does not need to wait for, say "I'd put that on a queue", and mention retries and idempotency in the same breath.
sections.pitfall: Assuming every message is processed exactly once. With at-least-once delivery, a consumer that is not idempotent sends two emails or charges twice.

check.question: Why must queue consumers usually be idempotent?
choices: Queues reorder the bytes inside each message
Idempotent code always runs faster
Queues require every consumer to be written in the same language
Most queues deliver at least once, so the same message can be processed more than once
check.explanation: If a worker crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging, the queue delivers the message again. Idempotent consumers make that second delivery harmless instead of sending a second email or charge.

sections.title: Worked design: a URL shortener
sections.key: A URL shortener is a read-heavy key lookup: base62 codes, a cache in front of replicated storage, and a 302 redirect when every click must be counted.
sections.body:
**Requirements.** Create a short link, redirect it, optional alias and expiry; accounts are out of scope. Redirects must be fast (under about 50 ms) and highly available, a link must never point to the wrong URL, and the service takes 100 million new links a month.

[[visual]]

**Codes.** Base62 (a to z, A to Z, 0 to 9) gives 62^7, about 3.5 trillion, 7-character codes:

[[visual 2]]

**API and data.** `POST /api/links {long_url}` returns `201 {code}`; `GET /{code}` returns `302 Location: ...`. Table `links(code PRIMARY KEY, long_url, created_at, expires_at)`: every read is a primary-key lookup.

[[visual 3]]

Popular links follow a power law, so a few gigabytes of cache absorb most redirects. Clicks go to a queue so analytics never slow the redirect.

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Estimates

steps.label: A month is about 2.6 million seconds

visual.result: Read-heavy, small records, simple key lookups: focus on the read path

rows: Counter + base62, ids handed to servers in blocks
no collisions, no coordination per request
sequential codes are guessable: they leak volume and allow enumeration
First 7 characters of a hash of the URL
the same URL always gets the same code
truncation collides: detect and resolve it

items.title: 301 Moved Permanently
points: Browsers may cache the redirect for a long time
Less traffic for you
Repeat clicks are invisible, and the link is hard to change or expire

items.title: 302 Found (temporary)
points: Every click passes through your servers
You can count clicks
You can change or expire the link

sections.tip: Close with failure modes: "If Redis dies, reads fall back to the replicas; if the leader dies, creating links pauses until failover, but redirects keep working."
sections.pitfall: Choosing 301 without thinking. Browsers may cache it for a long time, so for those users you can no longer change or expire the link, or count their clicks.

check.question: Why does this design concentrate on the read path?
choices: Writes are handled entirely by the CDN
Reads cost more to store than writes
Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1, so redirects dominate the load
Interviewers only ever ask about reads
check.explanation: The estimates show about 40 writes per second against about 4,000 reads. Caching and replicas for redirects therefore matter far more than optimizing link creation.

sections.title: Worked design: a news feed
sections.key: Feeds are read-heavy: push new posts into precomputed feeds for normal accounts, pull celebrity posts at read time, and run the fan-out through a queue.
sections.body:
Users follow others and see recent posts, newest first. 50 million daily users open the feed 10 times a day: 500M reads, about 5,000 per second (15,000 at peak), against about 50 posts per second. Each read merges posts from about 200 followed accounts, so building feeds is the expensive part.

**API.** `POST /posts` and `GET /feed?cursor=...&limit=20`. Use a **cursor**, not an offset: new posts arrive constantly, so offsets shift and repeat items.

[[visual]]

**The hybrid**: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities. Workers fed by a queue do the fan-out, so posting stays fast. A post appearing three seconds late harms nobody, so feeds can be eventually consistent.

[[code]]

items.title: Fan-out on read (pull)
points: At read time, fetch recent posts from everyone followed and merge
Cheap writes; nothing precomputed for inactive users
Slow feed loads for users who follow many accounts

items.title: Fan-out on write (push)
points: On each post, workers push its id into every follower's feed list (a Redis list trimmed to 800)
Reading a feed is one fast lookup
A celebrity with 30 million followers means 30 million inserts per post

sections.code:
def fan_out(post_id, author):  # worker
    if is_celebrity(author):
        return               # pulled later
    for f in followers(author):
        r.lpush(f"feed:{f}", post_id)
        r.ltrim(f"feed:{f}", 0, 799)

def get_feed(user, cursor):
    ids = r.lrange(f"feed:{user}", 0, 199)
    ids += celebrity_posts(user)  # pull
    ids = newest_first(ids, after=cursor)
    return hydrate(ids[:20])  # post cache
sections.deeper: Deep dives worth offering: store feed entries as post ids and hydrate the content from a post cache, so an edited or deleted post is fixed in one place; rank instead of pure recency (collect candidate posts, score them, sort); and recover when the feed cache is lost by rebuilding on read with fan-out on read, then repopulating the lists.
sections.tip: Contrast consistency needs out loud: "If Bob sees Alice's post three seconds late, nobody is hurt. A payment is different."
sections.pitfall: Choosing pure fan-out on write and forgetting celebrities. A single post from an account with 30 million followers becomes 30 million writes.

check.question: Why do real feed systems use a hybrid of push and pull?
choices: Pull is always faster than push for every user
Pushing a post from an account with millions of followers is too expensive, so those posts are pulled at read time while normal accounts are pushed
Push loses posts whenever the queue is full
A hybrid design removes the need for any cache
check.explanation: Push makes reads cheap but its cost grows with follower count, which explodes for celebrities. Pulling only those few accounts at read time keeps both reads and writes manageable.

keyTerms.definition: How well the system must work: latency, availability, scale, consistency.
Queries (requests) per second; estimate as daily count divided by about 10^5.
Spreads requests across a pool of servers and stops sending to ones that fail health checks.
A server that keeps no per-user state locally, so any instance can handle any request.
Read from the cache, fill it from the database on a miss, and delete the key when data changes.
Time to live: how long a cached entry is kept before it expires.
A network of edge servers that cache static content close to users.
The delay before a follower database reflects a write made on the leader.
The field that decides which database shard holds a row; it should match the main access pattern.
During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.
A rate-limiting algorithm that allows bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing an average rate.
Pushing each new post into every follower's precomputed feed at write time.

summary: Drive the interview: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, trade-offs.
Estimate with 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds, size for peak, and say what the numbers imply.
Stateless servers behind a health-checking load balancer scale out; cache-aside with TTLs and a CDN absorb reads.
Replicas lag, shard keys must match the access pattern, and partitions force consistency or availability per feature.
Queues need idempotent consumers; token buckets limit request rates.
URL shortener: base62 codes, cache-heavy reads, 302 for analytics. News feed: push for most, pull for celebrities.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Walk a friend through designing a URL shortener for 100 million new links a month: your estimates, how you generate codes, and how a redirect stays fast even when a cache server fails.

questions.question: Put the steps of a system design interview in a sensible order.
items: Draw the high-level design and trace a request
Deep dive into the hardest components
Discuss trade-offs, bottlenecks and failure modes
questions.explanation: Requirements and estimates shape everything after them, the API and data model come before the boxes and arrows, and deep dives and trade-offs come last, once there is a design to dig into.

questions.question: Which of these are non-functional requirements for a URL shortener? Select all that apply.
choices: Redirects complete in under 50 ms at the 99th percentile
Users can choose a custom alias
The service stays up if one data center fails
Links can expire on a chosen date
It handles 10,000 redirects per second at peak
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe how well the system works: latency, availability, scale. Custom aliases and expiry are features, so they are functional requirements.

questions.question: Twenty minutes into the interview, you realize you never asked how many users the system must support. What is the best move?
choices: Keep going, since scale questions are optional
Assume billions of users and add sharding everywhere
Ask the interviewer to choose the database instead
Pause, ask, and adjust the design to the answer
questions.explanation: Scale changes the design, and interviewers reward candidates who notice gaps and adapt. Assuming the maximum leads to an over-engineered design you cannot justify.

questions.question: An app has 50 million daily active users, each making 20 requests a day. Using 1 day ≈ 100,000 seconds, how many requests per second is that on average?
questions.explanation: 50M x 20 = 1 billion requests a day. 1,000,000,000 / 100,000 = 10,000 requests per second.

questions.question: Users upload 1 million photos a day at 2 MB each. About how many terabytes of new storage is that per year (365 days), before replication? Give the number of TB.
questions.explanation: 1M x 2 MB = 2 TB a day, and 2 TB x 365 = 730 TB a year. With three replicas you would plan for about 2.2 PB.

questions.question: A service averages 2,000 requests per second, and peaks are about 3 times the average. How many requests per second should you plan for at peak?
questions.explanation: 2,000 x 3 = 6,000 requests per second. Size the system for the peak, not the average, or it falls over at the busiest moment of the day.

questions.question: Peak load is 30,000 requests per second, and load tests show one app server comfortably handles 2,000. How many app servers do you need at peak, before adding headroom for failures?
questions.explanation: 30,000 / 2,000 = 15 servers. In practice you add headroom, for example a few extra servers so losing one or two, or a whole zone, does not overload the rest.

questions.question: A request makes 3 sequential calls to a service on another continent (about 100 ms round trip each) and 20 cache reads inside the data center (about 0.5 ms each). Roughly where does the time go?
choices: The cache reads dominate, at about 300 ms
Both take about the same time, roughly 150 ms each
The cross-continent calls dominate, about 300 ms against about 10 ms
Neither matters; the total is under 20 ms
questions.explanation: 3 x 100 ms = about 300 ms for the cross-continent calls, against 20 x 0.5 ms = about 10 ms for the cache reads. Cut or parallelize the remote calls first; tuning the cache would barely matter.

questions.question: After adding a load balancer and a second app server, users get logged out at random. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Sessions are stored in each server's memory, so requests landing on the other server find no session
The load balancer removes cookies from requests
Health checks log users out every few seconds
Round robin encrypts cookies differently on each server
questions.explanation: Each server keeps its own in-memory sessions, so a request that lands on the other server finds no session. Move sessions to a shared store such as Redis, or use signed tokens.

questions.question: Some requests to your service take 20 ms and others take 5 seconds. Which load balancing algorithm usually spreads the load better than round robin here?
choices: Random choice
Least connections
Round robin with more servers
Hashing on the request URL
questions.explanation: Round robin ignores how busy each server is, so one server can pile up slow requests. Least connections sends new work to the server with the fewest requests in flight.

questions.question: Instead of moving sessions to Redis, a teammate proposes sticky sessions on the load balancer. What is the main downside?
choices: Sticky sessions require HTTP/3 on every client
Load can become uneven, and when a server dies its users lose their sessions
They make TLS termination impossible
They double the number of database writes
questions.explanation: Pinning users to servers makes load uneven (a few heavy users can swamp one machine) and ties each session's fate to one server, so a crash or deploy logs those users out.

questions.question: Complete the cache-aside read path so a miss fills the cache.
choices: redis.delete(key)
db.update_user(user_id, user)
redis.set(key, json.dumps(user), ex=300)
return json.loads(cached)
questions.explanation: On a miss, load from the database, store the result with a TTL so it expires on its own, and return it. Deleting the key or writing to the database belong to the write path, not the read path.

questions.question: What is wrong with this update path?
questions.code:
def update_price(product_id, new_price):
    redis.set(f"product:{product_id}:price", new_price)      # no TTL
    db.execute("UPDATE products SET price = %s WHERE id = %s",
               (new_price, product_id))
choices: redis.set cannot store numeric values
The UPDATE statement must run before the function is called
Prices are sensitive data and must never be cached
The cache is written before the database and has no TTL, so a failed UPDATE leaves a never-saved price cached indefinitely
questions.explanation: The cache is written first, with no TTL. If the UPDATE fails or the process crashes before it, the cache serves a price that was never saved, and without a TTL it does so indefinitely. Write the database first, then delete the cache key, and give entries a TTL.

questions.question: A key read 20,000 times a second expires, and database CPU jumps to 100% for several seconds. What is this, and what helps?
choices: Replication lag; send all reads to the leader
A memory leak in Redis; restart it on a schedule
A cache stampede; let one request rebuild the value while others wait or get the stale copy, and jitter TTLs
An N+1 query problem; use eager loading
questions.explanation: Thousands of simultaneous misses on one hot key is a cache stampede. Let one request rebuild the value (a lock or request coalescing) while others wait or get the old copy, and jitter TTLs so hot keys do not expire together.

questions.question: What does a CDN do for your site's images and JavaScript files?
choices: Compresses and indexes your database
Balances writes across database shards
Encrypts your files at rest
Serves cached copies from servers near each user, cutting latency and load on your servers
questions.explanation: CDN edge servers cache static files close to users, so requests travel a short distance and never reach your servers. It does not touch your database or encryption at rest.

questions.question: Why do sites name assets like `app.3f9a1c.js` and let CDNs cache them for a year?
choices: A new version gets a new filename, so long caching is safe and updates take effect immediately
Browsers refuse to cache files without a hash in the name
The hash encrypts the file so the CDN cannot read it
CDNs only accept files whose names contain a hash
questions.explanation: The hash changes whenever the content changes, so a new deploy references a new filename. Old files can be cached forever because they never change, and users still get updates immediately.

questions.question: A read-heavy app's database is at 90% CPU, almost all of it from SELECT queries. What is the most direct first fix?
choices: Shard the database by user id right away
Add read replicas and send reads to them, with a cache for hot data
Put a bigger load balancer in front of the app servers
Drop indexes so the database has less to maintain
questions.explanation: Read replicas (plus a cache for hot data) add read capacity without the complexity of sharding. Sharding is for when writes or total data outgrow one machine.

questions.question: You shard a chat app's messages across 16 databases. Most reads load the latest 50 messages of one conversation. Which shard key fits best?
choices: The message timestamp, ranged by day
sender_id, so each user's messages are together
conversation_id, hashed, so each conversation lives on one shard
A random number per message, for perfect balance
questions.explanation: Hashing conversation_id keeps each conversation on one shard, so the main query touches one database, while different conversations spread evenly. Timestamps create a hot shard for today, and sender_id or random keys scatter a conversation across shards.

questions.question: During a network partition, which of these features should refuse or delay requests rather than risk stale or conflicting data? Select all that apply.
choices: Deducting a payment from a wallet balance
Selling the last seat on a flight
Showing a post's like count
Loading a news feed
Reserving a unique username
questions.explanation: Money, a single scarce seat and globally unique names break if two sides of a partition both say yes. Like counts and feeds can be briefly stale and converge later.

questions.question: Explain the CAP theorem in plain terms.
questions.answer: When a network partition splits a distributed system, each side must choose: refuse requests it cannot confirm are current (consistency) or keep answering with possibly stale data (availability). Without a partition you can have both; the everyday trade-off is latency versus consistency.
questions.explanation: Interviewers prefer this practical version over the acronym: name the partition, the choice, and which features need which side.

questions.question: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Accepts every write and streams changes to the others
Applies the leader's changes and serves reads
The delay before a follower reflects a recent write
Promoting a follower when the leader dies
One database holding only a subset of the rows

questions.explanation: The leader takes writes, followers copy them and serve reads, lag is how far behind they are, failover replaces a dead leader, and a shard holds only part of the data.

questions.question: Which task is the best candidate to move onto a queue and a background worker?
choices: Checking the password during login
Reading a product's price to render the page
Sending a welcome email after signup
Validating that a form field is not empty
questions.explanation: The user does not need to wait for the welcome email, and it can be retried if the email service is down. The other tasks are needed to answer the current request.

questions.question: The queue delivers at least once. Customers sometimes receive two 'Your order shipped' emails. What is wrong with this consumer?
questions.code:
def handle(message):
    order = db.get_order(message["order_id"])
    send_email(order.customer_email, "Your order shipped!")
    db.execute("UPDATE orders SET shipped_email_sent = true WHERE id = %s",
               (order.id,))
    queue.ack(message)
choices: It never checks shipped_email_sent before sending, so a redelivered message sends the email again
ack must be called before the order is read
The UPDATE should be an INSERT
send_email cannot be called from a worker
questions.explanation: If the worker crashes after sending the email but before the UPDATE or ack, the message is redelivered and the email goes out again. Check shipped_email_sent first (ideally claim it atomically with an UPDATE ... WHERE shipped_email_sent = false) so a repeat does nothing. Acking first would instead risk never sending the email.

questions.question: A client's token bucket holds up to 10 tokens and is full. It refills at 2 tokens per second. At t = 0, 25 requests arrive at the same instant. How many are rejected?
questions.explanation: The full bucket allows a burst of 10, and no time has passed for any refill, so the other 15 are rejected with 429. One second later, 2 more requests would be allowed.

questions.question: A limiter allows 100 requests per minute using fixed windows that reset on the minute. What is the most requests a client can get through within about 2 seconds?
questions.explanation: The client sends 100 at 0:59 (the end of one window) and 100 at 1:00 (the start of the next): 200 in about two seconds, double the intended rate. Sliding windows and token buckets avoid this.

questions.question: Codes use base62 characters (a to z, A to Z, 0 to 9). What is the shortest code length that gives at least 1 billion distinct codes?
questions.explanation: 62^5 is about 916 million, just short of a billion. 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, so 6 characters are enough. 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion.

questions.question: A shortener creates 100 million links a month, and each link is read 100 times for every write. Assuming a month has 2.5 million seconds, how many redirects per second is that on average?
questions.explanation: Writes: 100M / 2.5M s = 40 per second. Reads: 40 x 100 = 4,000 redirects per second, before applying a peak factor.

questions.question: The product team wants click counts for every short link. Which redirect status should the service return?
choices: 301, so browsers cache the redirect
302, so every click passes through your servers and can be counted
200 with the long URL in the body
404 followed by a JavaScript redirect
questions.explanation: With 302, browsers come back to you on every click, so each one can be counted. 301 lets browsers cache the redirect and skip your server, so repeat clicks vanish from analytics.

questions.question: A design uses the first 7 characters of the long URL's MD5 hash as the short code. What must the design handle?
choices: Nothing, because MD5 never produces collisions
Codes that are longer than 7 characters
Collisions: different URLs can share the same 7-character prefix, so inserts must detect and resolve them
Codes that change every time the same URL is hashed
questions.explanation: Truncating a hash to 7 characters makes collisions between different URLs possible, and their likelihood grows with billions of links, so inserts must detect a taken code and resolve it (for example by rehashing with a salt). Hashing is deterministic, so the same URL always gives the same code.

questions.question: With pure fan-out on write, what happens when an account with 30 million followers posts?
choices: The post is rejected for being too popular
Nothing special; push cost does not depend on follower count
Followers must refresh twice to see it
One post triggers about 30 million feed inserts, delaying fan-out and wasting work
questions.explanation: Push cost is proportional to follower count, so one post means about 30 million feed inserts. Fan-out lags, workers are swamped, and much of the work goes to feeds of users who will not log in today.

questions.question: Why does the feed API use cursor pagination rather than offsets?
choices: New posts arrive constantly, so offsets shift and cause duplicates; a cursor marks exactly where the last page ended
Offsets cannot be used with Redis lists
HTTP/2 requires cursors for all list endpoints
Offsets reveal other users' ids
questions.explanation: New posts keep arriving at the top, so offset-based pages shift and show duplicates or skip posts. A cursor marks exactly where the previous page ended.

questions.question: Which statements about the hybrid feed design are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Posts from normal accounts are pushed into followers' precomputed feeds
Celebrity posts are merged in at read time
Fan-out runs in background workers fed by a queue
Every feed read queries the posts of all 200 followed accounts
Feeds must be strongly consistent across all replicas
questions.explanation: Normal accounts are pushed by background workers, and celebrity posts are pulled and merged at read time. Feeds are deliberately eventually consistent, and reads do not query all 200 followees.
